title: Zubin Mehta Walks Away from Israel — Then Walks Back
excerpt: The Indian-born maestro's protest cancellation and quiet reversal tell a story about the impossible choices facing artists with deep ties on both sides
body:
In January 2026, Zubin Mehta did something he had never done in more than five decades of conducting the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra: he cancelled. All of his 2026 engagements in Israel, gone — wiped from the schedule in a single announcement that sent shockwaves through the classical music world.

**"I cannot separate music from politics,"** the 89-year-old Indian-born conductor told India Today, in a rare departure from the diplomatic ambiguity that had defined his public statements for years. "I have cancelled all my commitments in Israel this year because of my opposition to the way Netanyahu is handling the Palestinian issue as a whole."

**The weight of that statement is hard to overstate.** Mehta's relationship with the Israel Philharmonic is not merely professional — it is existential. He first conducted the orchestra in 1961, became its music director in 1977, and was named Music Director for Life in 1981, a title no other conductor holds anywhere in the world. He led the orchestra during the Six-Day War. He performed in the ruins of the Berlin Wall. He won the Israel Prize. To say Mehta is embedded in the Israeli cultural establishment is like saying the Ganges runs through Varanasi — technically accurate but absurdly understated.

**His cancellation was read as a moral earthquake.** The European Palestinian Council for Political Relations called it "one of the strongest public positions taken by a global cultural figure with long-standing ties to the Israeli cultural establishment." Artists and intellectuals who had long argued for cultural boycotts of Israel pointed to Mehta as proof that even the most deeply invested voices could no longer stay silent. The conductor himself went further, telling interviewers that artists have a "moral responsibility to take a stand on major issues, particularly those involving wars and crimes against peoples."

**And then, quietly, he reversed course.** By May, reports surfaced that Mehta had agreed to return to conduct the Israel Philharmonic in 2027. No press conference, no public statement explaining the change. Norman Lebrecht, the influential classical music commentator, noted in The Critic that the maestro "severed ties with Israel in 2026, protesting Netanyahu's policies, though he later reversed his stance."

**The reversal has received a fraction of the coverage that the cancellation did** — a pattern familiar to anyone who has watched the dynamics of cultural boycotts play out. The dramatic gesture makes news; the quiet walk-back does not. For critics of the boycott movement, the reversal proves that even Mehta found the position untenable. For supporters, the initial cancellation remains the meaningful act — a marker laid down by a man who had every reason to stay silent.

**For India's diaspora, the story carries particular resonance.** Mehta is Parsi, born in Bombay in 1936, and remains one of the most celebrated Indian-born figures in Western classical music. His career has been a source of quiet pride for the Indian community, particularly in the arts — proof that Indian musicians could command the world's great orchestras. His decision to protest was covered extensively in Indian media, with many NRI commentators drawing parallels to diaspora debates about when cultural engagement becomes complicity.

**The question Mehta's episode poses is one that diaspora Indians encounter repeatedly:** How do you maintain relationships across political fault lines? The Indian community in Israel, though small, is growing. Indian tech workers in Tel Aviv, students at Hebrew University, yoga instructors in Haifa — all navigate the same tension Mehta confronted: genuine personal connection to a place whose government's actions they may find unconscionable.

**Mehta will turn 90 next April.** Whether his 2027 return to the podium in Tel Aviv becomes his final statement or merely the latest chapter in a career defined by impossible balancing acts, the episode has already served its purpose: it forced a conversation that most cultural figures would rather avoid.
